$comment: Generated by scripts/generate-envelope-vectors.mjs with node:crypto (OpenSSL), deliberately NOT with the library any of the three implementations use. Read by Jest, JUnit and the Swift parity harness. Each rejection names the refusal all three must answer with. Do not hand-edit.

vectors.name: ascii-request-body
vectors.proves: the ordinary case: a JSON request body the assistant endpoint would accept
vectors.plaintext: {"message":"what can I cook with two eggs","languageCode":"en"}

vectors.name: turkish-multibyte
vectors.proves: UTF-8 is the encoding, not the platform default. An implementation that reaches for UTF-16 or a locale encoding produces a different ciphertext here and the same one for the ASCII case above.
vectors.plaintext: {"message":"İki yumurtayla ne pişirebilirim? Şöyle düşün: çöğen, ğ.","languageCode":"tr"}

vectors.name: response-envelope
vectors.proves: the direction the native side DECRYPTS: a backend success envelope, `{ data: ... }`

vectors.name: empty-object
vectors.proves: a 2-byte plaintext still produces a 18-byte sealed payload — the tag is appended, never folded in

vectors.name: long-body
vectors.proves: more than one AES block, so a single-block shortcut in any implementation shows up

rejects.name: tampered-auth-tag
rejects.proves: the GCM tag is verified, not carried. Decrypting this must fail rather than return bytes.

rejects.name: iv-too-short
rejects.proves: an 11-byte IV is rejected BY THE LENGTH CHECK, before the cipher sees it. Each implementation has its own opinion about a short nonce — one refuses it, one tolerates it and fails the tag — so only the named refusal tells them apart.

rejects.name: payload-shorter-than-tag
rejects.proves: a sealed payload that cannot even hold a tag is rejected as malformed, and named as such — without the check Swift traps on a negative prefix and the others report a tag failure
